To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the simulated seasonality and burden of BC in the Arctic are strongly influenced by scavenging of the BC in the lower atmosphere, and that this influence is strongest for lower tropospheric BC.
the simulated annual cycles of BC transport, deposition, and concentrations are strongly influenced by the simulated seasonality and strength of wet deposition.

the seasonality of simulated BC concentrations is driven by the seasonality of transport of BC from mid-latitudes, and that scavenging of convective clouds in mid-latitudes has the largest effect on simulated BC concentrations in the lower troposphere in the Arctic.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the processes that determine the seasonality of Arctic BC concentrations.
the seasonality of Arctic black carbon and its processes.
the seasonality of global and local BC transport, emissions and deposition in the Arctic and their influence on the vertical distribution of BC.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the models have a similar seasonality of BC processes but differ in magnitude and timing of BC deposition and burden, and that convective scavaging is an important process for Arctic BC deposition.
all models have similar seasonality of BC wet deposition, but the models differ in magnitude of the simulated BC wet deposition.
the models simulate similar seasonal cycles in BC transport to the Arctic, but differ substantially in BC burdens, vertical distributions and residence time in the Arctic.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the simulated BC seasonality in the Arctic is largely driven by BC transport from lower latitude sources and that the seasonality of Arctic BC wet deposition is largely driven by scavenging in Arctic stratiform clouds.

the Arctic BC burden is sensitive to the simulated seasonality in BC emissions, deposition, and transport, which in turn depends on the simulated seasonality and strength of the Arctic boundary layer circulation and on the strength of the Arctic surface temperature inversion, as well as the seasonality and strength in the Arctic surface albedo feedback.
the seasonality of Arctic BC processes is strongly influenced by BC wet deposition in convective clouds, with the largest effect being on BC burdens and vertical profiles in the Arctic.
The main takeaway from our work is that
BC transport from lower to higher latitudes is an important process that must be considered in future model development and in the interpretation of observations.
the simulated seasonality and strength of the annual cycle of BC in the Arctic is highly dependent on the simulated seasonality, strength, and vertical distribution of wet and dry deposition of BC.
the simulated Arctic BC burden and seasonal cycle are highly dependent on how BC is scavenged in convective and stratiform clouds.
